title: AI & Algorithms Fundamentals
description: A tour through the core ideas behind modern AI systems -- reinforcement learning, search, embeddings, and the training dynamics that make models work.
learningObjectives: Explain how Q-learning picks actions by comparing expected future reward
Understand why time-expanded search graphs are needed for moving obstacles
Trace how A* uses f(n) = g(n) + h(n) to choose which node to expand next
Describe what word embeddings capture through vector arithmetic
Compare the guarantees BFS and DFS give on unweighted graphs
Identify the risk of ignoring path cost in greedy best-first search
Explain how Minimax models a worst-case rational opponent
Recognize how learning rate affects gradient descent stability
Diagnose overfitting from a train/test accuracy gap
Explain why epsilon-greedy agents sometimes explore instead of exploit

questions.description:
An AI agent is navigating traffic using Reinforcement Learning. Its environment model predicts a truck will pass directly in front of it on the next tick.

Which action maximizes its future reward (Q-value)?

options.label: A) Forward  [Q: -100]
options.explanation: Incorrect. Q: -100 means the model predicts a collision. An agent maximizing expected reward never picks the lowest-value action on purpose.

options.label: B) Wait  [Q: +10]
options.explanation: Correct! Q-learning always picks the action with the highest expected future reward. +10 (survive) beats -100 (collide), -5, and -5.

options.label: C) Left  [Q: -5]
options.explanation: Incorrect. -5 is better than -100, but it's still lower than the +10 available by waiting.

options.label: D) Right  [Q: -5]
options.explanation: Incorrect. Same issue as Left -- -5 loses to the +10 Q-value of waiting.

questions.description:
A lane looks blocked right now, but the car in it moves at a constant speed, so its position at any future moment can be predicted. Plain BFS on a static grid can't express "wait, then go."

What kind of search graph lets the algorithm plan around moving traffic like this?

options.label: A) Static-grid BFS
options.explanation: Incorrect. A plain static grid treats each cell as always blocked or always open -- it has no notion of a cell becoming safe later.

options.label: B) Time-expanded BFS
options.explanation: Correct! Searching over (cell, tick) pairs instead of just cells lets the algorithm treat 'safe at time t' as its own fact, so waiting a beat then moving becomes a normal move.

options.label: C) Random restarts
options.explanation: Incorrect. Randomly retrying gives no guarantee of finding a safe route and ignores the predictable motion of the traffic entirely.

options.label: D) Flood fill
options.explanation: Incorrect. Flood fill just labels connected regions of a static map -- it has no concept of time or moving obstacles.

questions.description:
A* picks which tile to expand next using f(n) = g(n) + h(n), where g(n) is the cost so far and h(n) is a heuristic estimate (often Manhattan distance) to the goal.

Between two frontier tiles, which one does A* expand next?

options.label: A) The tile with the lowest f(n)
options.explanation: Correct! A* always expands the frontier node with the smallest f(n) = g(n) + h(n) -- that's what guarantees it finds the optimal path when h(n) never overestimates.

options.label: B) The tile with the highest g(n)
options.explanation: Incorrect. Highest g(n) means the most expensive path so far -- that's the opposite of what a cost-minimizing search wants.

options.label: C) Whichever tile is physically closest to the start
options.explanation: Incorrect. That ignores h(n) entirely and would just reduce to uninformed search outward from the start.

options.label: D) A random unexpanded tile
options.explanation: Incorrect. A* is not random -- it's a deterministic best-first search driven by f(n).

questions.description:
AI converts words into vectors (embeddings) so that words used in similar contexts land close together in vector space. A classic demonstration:

vector("king") − vector("man") + vector("woman") = ?

options.label: A) queen
options.explanation: Correct! Embeddings encode relationships like gender and royalty as directions in vector space -- removing 'man' and adding 'woman' shifts king's vector right next to queen's.

options.label: B) apple
options.explanation: Incorrect. 'apple' isn't used in similar contexts to royalty or gender terms, so it sits in a totally different region of embedding space.

options.label: C) bicycle
options.explanation: Incorrect. Word vectors come from co-occurrence patterns in text -- 'bicycle' rarely appears near 'king', 'man', or 'woman'.

options.label: D) shouting
options.explanation: Incorrect. That's an action, not the gender/royalty pattern this vector arithmetic captures.

questions.description:
Both Breadth-First Search and Depth-First Search are uninformed -- they use no heuristic at all.

Which one is guaranteed to find the shortest path (fewest edges) in an unweighted graph?

options.label: A) BFS
options.explanation: Correct! BFS explores level by level, so the first time it reaches the goal is guaranteed to be via the fewest possible edges.

options.label: B) DFS
options.explanation: Incorrect. DFS dives down one branch as far as it can -- it can find a valid path, but not necessarily the shortest one.

options.label: C) Both, always
options.explanation: Incorrect. Only BFS carries the shortest-path guarantee on unweighted graphs; DFS does not.

options.label: D) Neither
options.explanation: Incorrect. BFS does guarantee the shortest path in an unweighted graph -- that's exactly why it's used for that job.

questions.description:
Greedy best-first search expands whichever node looks closest to the goal right now, using only h(n) -- it ignores g(n), the cost already paid.

What's the main risk of ignoring g(n) like this?

options.label: A) It can lock onto a path that looks promising early but is actually longer overall
options.explanation: Correct! Because it never accounts for cost-so-far, greedy search can commit to a route that seemed close to the goal but turns out far more expensive than an alternative.

options.label: B) It always runs slower than BFS
options.explanation: Incorrect. Greedy search is often faster than BFS in practice since the heuristic focuses the search -- speed isn't the core issue.

options.label: C) It uses more memory than Dijkstra's algorithm
options.explanation: Incorrect. Memory usage isn't the defining risk here -- optimality is.

options.label: D) There's no real downside
options.explanation: Incorrect. Ignoring path cost so far is exactly why greedy best-first search isn't guaranteed to be optimal.

questions.description:
In a two-player adversarial game, Minimax assumes your opponent always plays their best possible move against you.

When it's the opponent's turn to move in the game tree, which value does Minimax assume they'll pick?

options.label: A) The move that minimizes your score
options.explanation: Correct! Minimax alternates: on your turn it picks the max value for you, and on the opponent's turn it assumes they pick the value that's worst (minimum) for you.

options.label: B) The move that maximizes your score
options.explanation: Incorrect. That's what Minimax assumes on your turn, not the opponent's -- a rational adversary wouldn't help you.

options.label: C) A random legal move
options.explanation: Incorrect. Minimax models a worst-case, perfectly rational opponent, not a random one.

options.label: D) Whatever move you'd pick in their position
options.explanation: Incorrect. The opponent's goal is the opposite of yours, so they optimize for your minimum, not mirror your choice.

questions.description:
Gradient descent updates a model's weights by stepping opposite the gradient of the loss function, scaled by a learning rate.

What typically happens if the learning rate is set far too high?

options.label: A) The updates overshoot and the loss can bounce around or diverge
options.explanation: Correct! Too large a step can jump right past the minimum each time, so instead of converging smoothly the loss oscillates or even grows.

options.label: B) Training converges instantly to the perfect solution
options.explanation: Incorrect. A very high learning rate usually causes instability, not instant perfect convergence.

options.label: C) The learning rate has no effect on training
options.explanation: Incorrect. The learning rate directly controls the size of every weight update -- it has a big effect.

options.label: D) Training always becomes slower, never unstable
options.explanation: Incorrect. Too small a learning rate makes training slow; too large a one makes it unstable -- these are opposite failure modes.

questions.description:
A model scores 99% accuracy on its training data but only 61% on new, unseen data.

What does this gap between training and test performance usually indicate?

options.label: A) Overfitting -- it memorized the training data instead of learning general patterns
options.explanation: Correct! A big gap between training and test accuracy is the classic signature of overfitting: the model fit noise and specifics of the training set that don't generalize.

options.label: B) Underfitting -- the model is too simple
options.explanation: Incorrect. Underfitting shows up as poor performance on training data too -- here training accuracy is very high.

options.label: C) The model is performing perfectly
options.explanation: Incorrect. A 38-point drop on unseen data is a strong warning sign, not a sign of success.

options.label: D) The training hardware was faulty
options.explanation: Incorrect. This is a statistical pattern about generalization, not a hardware issue.

questions.description:
An epsilon-greedy agent picks the best-known action most of the time, but occasionally picks a random action instead.

Why would an agent ever deliberately choose a random, possibly worse-looking action?

options.label: A) To explore, in case an unvisited action is actually better than what it currently believes is best
options.explanation: Correct! Without occasional exploration, the agent could get stuck exploiting an action that only looks best because it hasn't tried the better ones yet.

options.label: B) It's a bug in the algorithm
options.explanation: Incorrect. The randomness is deliberate -- it's the 'epsilon' in epsilon-greedy, not a malfunction.

options.label: C) Random actions are always secretly optimal
options.explanation: Incorrect. Random actions aren't assumed optimal -- they're tried precisely because their value is uncertain.

options.label: D) The player told it to move randomly
options.explanation: Incorrect. This is an internal exploration strategy the agent runs on its own, independent of player input.
